<reason>A wins a competitive debate by better distinguishing protection of shared space from punishment without feasible alternatives. B’s place-specific restrictions and concentration-risk arguments were substantial. But A explicitly permitted clearing obstructing tents and enforcing safety requirements against recurrence, while B continued portraying its position as indefinite tolerance. A also directly answered the accessibility question; B largely repeated the preference-veto objection. B’s dispersal mechanism did not adequately weigh displacement and disrupted support against local gains.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s playground answer conceded necessary clearance while observing that sweeps also cannot guarantee against reoccupation. This undercut B’s prevention-versus-restoration contrast: B needed to show why enforceable access and safety rules were insufficient, rather than repeatedly asserting that A left neighbors without recourse.</best_rebuttal>
